title: When the Drink Becomes the Place You Go to Escape Your Life, Something Deeper Is Asking for Help
paragraphs: When the Drink Becomes the Place You Go to Escape Your Life, Something Deeper Is Asking for Help

You may never call yourself an alcoholic. You may still go to work, pay the bills, love your family, laugh with friends, and sit in church on Sunday. But if alcohol has quietly become the place you run when being fully present in your own life hurts too much, the deepest question may not be how much you drink—but what you are trying so desperately not to feel.
There is a moment nobody sees.
The bottle opens.
The glass fills.
The first swallow goes down.
And for a little while, everything gets quieter.
Not fixed.
Just quieter.

The argument is still real. The marriage is still strained. The loneliness is still waiting. The bills did not disappear. The memory still happened. The grief still has your address. The shame still knows your name.
But for a few hours, maybe you do not have to feel all of it.
And that is precisely why this conversation is harder than simply saying, “Drinking is bad.”
Because sometimes the drink is not really about the drink.
Sometimes it is about escape.
Maybe nobody would look at you and think you have a problem.
You are functioning.
You show up.
You provide.
You answer messages.
You make people laugh.
Maybe you even serve at church.
And you certainly do not identify with the word “alcoholic.”
So when somebody starts talking about alcohol abuse, you immediately think, That isn't me.
Maybe it isn't.
Not everyone who drinks has alcohol use disorder, and Scripture does not teach that every use of wine is inherently sinful.
But there is another question worth asking.
When life hurts, where do you go?
When the house becomes quiet and your thoughts become loud, where do you go?
When disappointment sits on your chest...
when resentment begins boiling...
when you feel like a failure...
when the marriage feels cold...
when nobody knows how exhausted you really are...
when memories you thought you buried begin climbing out of their graves...
where do you go?
Because you can spend years debating whether you deserve a label while completely missing the refuge your heart has chosen.
And perhaps that is why Paul's words in Ephesians feel so piercing.
The Greek text says:
“καὶ μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ, ἐν ᾧ ἐστιν ἀσωτία, ἀλλὰ πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι”
“And do not get drunk with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit.”
— Ephesians 5:18
Look closely at the contrast.
Paul does not merely say, “Stop.”
He says, in effect, do not be filled this way; be filled another way.
Do not surrender yourself to intoxication.
Be filled with the Spirit.
That distinction matters.
The Greek verb translated “get drunk” is μεθύσκεσθε — methyskesthe, referring to becoming intoxicated or drunk.
Then Paul uses πληροῦσθε — plērousthe: “be filled.”
One influence increasingly takes possession of the person through intoxication.
Paul points believers toward another filling altogether: the Holy Spirit.
And between those two commands appears a sobering word:
ἀσωτία — asōtia.
It carries the sense of dissipation, reckless or wasteful living.
This same word family appears in the New Testament's description of the prodigal son's reckless life.
That makes Paul's contrast painfully relevant.
Because intoxication promises something it cannot finally deliver.
It says:
Come here. I'll make tonight easier.
Come here. You won't have to think about her.
Come here. You won't have to remember him.
Come here. You won't have to feel like a failure.
Come here. You can finally relax.
And perhaps, temporarily, you do.
That temporary relief is part of what makes escape so powerful.

Modern research on alcohol dependence recognizes something Scripture's wisdom should make Christians take seriously: people can use alcohol to cope with stress or emotional discomfort, and although drinking may provide temporary relief, that pattern can become part of a destructive cycle in which negative emotions and further drinking reinforce one another.
In other words, sometimes you are not chasing pleasure anymore.
You are running from pain.
And there is an enormous difference.
Maybe the question you need tonight is not:
“Am I an alcoholic?”
Maybe the question is:
“Why do I keep needing to leave myself?”
Read that again.
Why does sober reality sometimes feel like somewhere you cannot bear to stay?
What are you anesthetizing?
What are you trying not to remember?
Whose rejection still hurts?
What disappointment have you never grieved?
What secret shame follows you home?
What anger do you refuse to name?
What happened to you that you keep insisting “wasn't that bad”?
What are you afraid would happen if you sat completely sober before God and finally told Him the truth?
Because sometimes we keep trying to kill a thirst without asking what created it.
You pour another drink because sleep will not come.
But maybe sleep is not the deepest problem.
You drink because your nerves will not settle.
But maybe anxiety is knocking on a door you have kept locked for years.
You drink because your relationship is unbearable.
But perhaps alcohol has become easier than the conversation you know needs to happen.
You drink because you feel alone.
But eventually the thing you use to escape loneliness can begin isolating you even further.
You drink because you hate who you have become.
And then tomorrow morning, you hate yourself for drinking again.
So you promise:
Tonight will be different.
And sometimes it is.
Until another terrible day arrives.
Until another fight.
Another memory.
Another disappointment.
Another lonely night.
Then the old refuge whispers your name again.
This is where shame usually enters the story.
“You call yourself a Christian?”
“You prayed about this already.”
“You promised God you would stop.”
“Look at you.”
“Don't tell anyone.”
“They'll think you're a hypocrite.”
So you hide.
And hiding makes the darkness stronger.
But listen carefully:
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross so broken people could become better actors.
He came to save sinners.
The Gospel does not begin with pretending you are strong enough.
It begins with admitting that you are not.
Christian repentance is not theatrical self-hatred.
It is turning.
It is bringing what has been hidden into the light and agreeing with God about it.
Where drunkenness, deception, neglect, cruelty, irresponsibility, idolatry, or other sin has accompanied your drinking, repentance means refusing to rename darkness as harmless.
But biblical wisdom also refuses a shallow answer to a complicated human struggle.
Not every painful pattern is solved by shouting, “Try harder.”

Alcohol misuse can involve deeply established behavioral, emotional, social, and physical patterns. Some people need pastoral care. Some need Christian community. Some need counseling. Some need medical evaluation or professional addiction treatment. Some need all of these working together.
Seeking appropriate help is not a betrayal of faith.
Truth is not the enemy of faith.
Wisdom is not the enemy of faith.
And asking someone trustworthy to walk with you is not the opposite of depending on God.
Sometimes one of the most spiritually honest prayers a person can pray is:
Jesus, I cannot keep hiding this. Please help me tell somebody.

And if you have become physically dependent on alcohol, do not assume that abruptly stopping on your own is always safe. Alcohol withdrawal can become medically serious. Getting qualified medical guidance can be an act of wisdom, not weakness.
But even when treatment addresses the drinking, another question remains:
Where will your soul run now?
Because removing the bottle without discovering a deeper refuge can leave a frightening emptiness.
Paul's words do not end with:
“Do not get drunk.”
They continue:
“...but be filled with the Spirit.”
Christianity is not merely subtraction.
It is replacement.
Not merely stop running there.
Come here.
Not merely put down the counterfeit refuge.
Meet the real Refuge.
Jesus does not simply want to remove something from your hand while leaving your heart abandoned.
He calls you to Himself.
And no, that does not mean every craving instantly disappears when someone prays.
It does not mean recovery never includes relapse, counseling, accountability, treatment, tears, difficult conversations, changed routines, or painful consequences.
Grace is not magic language for pretending consequences do not exist.
Grace means your failure does not get the final word.
The cross does.
Think about Peter.
He swore that he would remain faithful.
Then pressure came.
Fear came.
And Peter denied Jesus three times.
Imagine the shame after the rooster crowed.
Peter had failed publicly and spiritually.
Yet the risen Jesus went looking for him.
Christ did not pretend Peter's denial did not matter.
He restored him.
He recommissioned him.
He transformed the site of failure into a testimony of grace.
That is what Jesus does.
He does not call evil good.
He overcomes evil with redemption.
He does not erase repentance.
He makes repentance a road home.
Maybe your scandal is hidden inside bottles nobody counts.
Maybe your family knows.
Maybe they have begged you.
Maybe your children have learned to recognize the difference between sober you and drinking you.
Maybe somebody you love has stopped believing your promises.

Maybe you have awakened with messages you regret sending, words you cannot retrieve, money you should not have spent, memories blurred around the edges, or apologies that are beginning to sound painfully familiar.
Or perhaps none of that has happened.
Perhaps nobody suspects anything.
Perhaps this struggle lives quietly behind a respectable life.
But God sees deeper than appearances.
And astonishingly, the One who sees everything is still calling you closer.
Not deeper into hiding.
Closer.
The Gospel says your worst chapter does not have authority to write your ending.
Jesus does.
This is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to one truth:
Not because your past was imaginary.
Not because consequences vanish.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because at Calvary, Jesus Christ took the guilt of sinners upon Himself, died, and rose again so that those who turn to Him in faith do not have to remain prisoners of who they were.
There is forgiveness.
There is reconciliation with God.
There is a new identity in Christ.
There is power to walk differently.
There is community.
There is wisdom.
There is help.
There is another way home.
Maybe tonight your first act of courage is not making a dramatic promise that you will never struggle again.
Maybe it is telling the truth.
Jesus, I have been using this to escape.
Jesus, I don't know how to face what I feel.
Jesus, I need help.
Jesus, forgive what is sinful in me.
Jesus, show me what I have been running from.
Jesus, lead me to people who can help me walk in the light.
That prayer may not feel spectacular.
But heaven has never required theatrical language from a repentant heart.
Come honestly.
Come exhausted.
Come ashamed.
Come confused.
Come with questions.
Come needing professional help.
Come needing accountability.
Come knowing that you have failed again.
Just stop believing the lie that you must become clean enough to approach the One who came precisely to rescue sinners.
And if this article exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to give strangers your entire story.
But you can take one small step out of isolation.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person fighting for another day.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who will never click an article titled “How to Know If You're an Alcoholic.”
They reject the label.
They insist they are fine.
But they know exactly what it means to pour a drink because they cannot bear another evening alone with their thoughts.
Send it privately to the person whose struggle should not become public conversation.
If this ministry is helping people encounter Scripture, repentance, grace, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ, there is also a practical way to stand behind the mission.
It helps us keep reaching the person scrolling at midnight.
The ashamed believer.
The exhausted parent.
The recovering addict.
The skeptic.
The prodigal.
The person who would never walk into a church today but might stop long enough to read about Jesus on a screen.
He is the point.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not merchandise.
Jesus Christ.
If you are drinking because you are trying to escape your life, perhaps the deepest invitation tonight is not merely to put down a glass.
It is to stop running alone.
Tell the truth to God.
Tell the truth to someone safe.
Seek appropriate professional help when it is needed.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive grace where shame tells you there can be none.
And begin learning what it means to take refuge in Christ rather than disappearing from your pain.
Because the bottle can make you forget for a night.
Jesus can teach you how to live in the light.
The bottle may temporarily numb what hurts.
Jesus can meet you inside what hurts.
The bottle offers escape.
Christ offers Himself.
And when morning comes, escape eventually asks you to pay for what it promised you last night.
Christ already paid at the cross for the sinner He came to redeem.
So tonight, before you reach automatically for whatever helps you disappear, ask yourself one question:
What am I actually trying to escape?
Then ask another:
What would happen if, instead of escaping, I brought it to Jesus and finally let someone help me carry it?
And comment.
Not for an algorithm alone.
“No more hiding.”
Maybe that is where your next chapter starts.
And remember this when the old refuge whispers again:
You do not need another place to disappear; in Jesus Christ, you have finally been given Someone to whom you can come home.
